title: MEP-CMAP Analyser
description:
MEP-CMAP Analyser is a BIDS-compliant, open-source, cross-platform desktop application for processing, quantifying and group-analysing transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and electromyography (EMG) neurophysiology recordings. It is built for researchers who need reproducible, auditable waveform analysis without writing custom scripts for every study.

The tool is not limited to a single measure or paradigm. It handles motor evoked potentials (MEPs), compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs), cortical silent periods (cSPs), M-wave recruitment curves, paired-pulse protocols such as short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) and intracortical facilitation (ICF), and any other time-locked EMG response measurable by peak-to-peak amplitude, onset latency or area under the curve. It operates on continuous recordings, pre-epoched trial stacks, and EMG bursts recorded without stimulation.

Capabilities

  • Direct import of Spike2, LabChart, EDF/BDF, AcqKnowledge and generic delimited text files, with a guided one-time wizard for arbitrary tabular layouts
  • Configurable filtering, including band-pass, notch and harmonic suppression, with live preview
  • Automated detection of response onset, offset and duration, peak-to-peak amplitude, root-mean-square amplitude, area under the curve and cortical silent period duration, each overridable per trial
  • Eight onset detection methods spanning derivative, derivative-ratio, amplitude-threshold, energy-operator and change-point approaches, with an optional median across them and per-trial reporting of how far they disagree
  • Automated outlier screening with an interactive review step, so exclusion decisions are explicit, persistent and recorded in the output
  • An interactive per-trial data inspector for marker adjustment, annotation and exclusion
  • Mmax normalisation with robust plateau detection across full recruitment curves, supramaximal clusters or a single M-wave
  • Compensation of evoked-potential magnitude for pre-stimulus spinal motoneurone excitability by quantile regression, following the method of Carson (2026, Journal of Physiology 604.14, 5731-5757), verified against the author's published reference implementation
  • Paired-pulse ratio computation with multiple reference assignments per file
  • Trial-level and summary CSV output, a group-level file formatted for linear mixed-effects modelling, per-trial waveform bundles, and BIDS-style derivatives with provenance

Changes in version 1.4.8

  • Outputs follow the BIDS layout for EMG derivatives. EMG became a BIDS datatype in BIDS 1.11, and BIDS derivatives mirror the raw layout inside a folder named for the pipeline that made them. Results and session files are now written to derivatives/mep-cmap-analyser/sub-XX/ses-YY/emg/, and the pipeline folder carries a dataset_description.json stating that it is a derivative dataset and which version of the tool produced it. Studies analysed earlier, in derivatives/sub-XX/ses-YY/, keep working: their sessions restore and the group analysis finds them. When such a recording is re-run, its copy in the old location is moved aside once the new session has been saved, so the group analysis does not count it twice, and File, Migrate study to BIDS layout moves a whole study at once after showing what will move. Nothing is deleted, and every move is recorded in a manifest.
  • Applied conditions can no longer reach another recording. Conditions are held as a list of events with their onset times. That list was kept when a different recording was opened, so analysing the second recording without reapplying its conditions cut its EMG at the first recording's stimulus times, and applying conditions to it merged the first recording's events into its events file, where they were read back on every later load. Conditions are now cleared when a recording is opened and are tied to the recording they were applied to, and a run warns when assigned events fall after the end of the recording. Any recording analysed after conditions had been applied to a different recording in the same sitting should have its _events.tsv deleted or checked and be re-run.
  • Stimulus types that cannot appear in a filename no longer stop a run. Spike2 marker codes between 32 and 126 are read as their ASCII character, so code 62 arrives as a greater-than sign and code 63 as a question mark, neither of which Windows accepts in a filename; the run failed part way through. Such characters are now encoded in filenames only, as %3E and %3F, while the stimulus type inside every output is unchanged. Onset-method figures for different stimulus types also stop overwriting one another, which the previous rule allowed by mapping several characters to the same name.
  • A file that fails is reported as failed. A recording that raised part way through still ended with All results saved and Analysis complete, was saved and was marked complete in the queue. The run now reports how many files failed, and a failed recording is neither saved nor marked complete.
  • The session is saved automatically after a run again. In 1.4.7 the automatic save failed with an error on every run, so work was saved only by Save Session.
  • The setup table lists only stimulus types with trials in the selected range. A type whose trials inside the range had all been excluded still appeared, from its events outside the range, although the analysis measured nothing for it.
  • The analysis can be run from a script. It relied on the graphical interface having loaded part of the plotting library first, so called on its own it failed at the first figure.

Changes in version 1.4.7

  • A whole study can be re-run from its saved sessions. A correction to how a value is computed previously reached only recordings analysed after it, and applying it to work already done meant reopening each recording, confirming each channel and running each analysis by hand; on a study of a hundred and thirty-five sessions that is a day's work in which the only thing that must not vary is the settings, and the settings are what a person re-entering them by hand will vary. The tool now plans the re-run first and reports what it found before anything is written: recordings whose saved session names a channel that the file no longer carries, recordings that have moved since they were analysed, and sessions whose analysis paused for outlier review, which cannot be answered with nobody present and are refused rather than run with the review skipped. Two sessions writing to one output are grouped and answered once rather than asked about repeatedly. Each file is compared against its own previous output afterwards, trial by trial, and a run is reported as complete only where it succeeded and its numbers held; columns that are new since the last run do not count as changes, while a value that moved, a column that vanished or a differing trial count do.
  • Outputs a later run has replaced can be archived. A group analysis reads every result file beneath a study, and nothing reconciles two files describing the same recording, so a session left holding both an older copy of its results and a newer one contributes twice: the same participant counted as two. This is easy to arrive at without noticing, since a change to how outputs are named or filed leaves the previous copies in place rather than overwriting them. The archive step is offered inside the same re-run dialogue rather than as a separate command, being part of the same job, and it may also be run alone for a study already re-run. What is current is decided by the saved session's own name, which is the same rule the re-run uses to pin its output, so the two cannot disagree about which files belong to a session. Superseded copies are moved rather than deleted, keeping their path relative to the study so where a file came from can be read from where it ended up, and a manifest records every move with the reason for it. A session with no current copy at all is never touched: its older output is the only one there is, and archiving it would remove the session from the analysis entirely rather than merely stop it counting twice. Those sessions are named, because they need re-running.
  • The reported onset latency is now the median across detectors where one is available. Which latency a file reported depended on which of eight onset detectors happened to be selected, and the detectors disagree; a study analysed with one and compared against a study analysed with another is comparing two definitions. The median across the member methods does not depend on that choice, and comparing the methods on every trial is now on by default so that the value is available rather than conditional on a setting most analysts never open. This makes onset detection slower, by roughly the number of member methods, which is the price of the reported value not depending on a preference. A marker placed by hand still takes precedence over both, a deliberate reading of a trace not being something an automatic median should overrule, and where no consensus is available the single selected detector is still used rather than the column being left empty. A new trial-level column, Latency_Source, records which of the three applied on each trial, because the fallback varies within a file and a latency column of mixed provenance cannot be pooled without saying so. The NIBS-DAS export carries the same field beside its latency, where the extended measures are enabled.
  • A cortical silent period duration is written only where the period was observed to end. Where the search window closed before the electromyogram returned, the duration reported was the distance to the window's edge, which reads as a short silent period rather than as one that was not measured. On a real study this removed two hundred and ten values that had been reported as durations of up to four hundred milliseconds; the remaining distribution runs from twenty-five to two hundred and ninety-eight milliseconds with a median of sixty-nine and a half.
  • Outlier review and per-stimulus-type figures are now off by default. Review halts an analysis to put flagged trials to the analyst, which no unattended run can answer; the separate figure per stimulus type is a diagnostic aid rather than an output most studies keep.

Note on latency and cortical silent period: values produced by version 1.4.6 and earlier were produced under different rules and should be re-run before they are reported. The detector version stamp changes to 2026-modular-v6, so a group analysis will refuse to pool outputs from before and after this release rather than combining values that no longer mean the same thing. The onset and offset detectors themselves are unchanged and reproduce the previous release exactly; what changed is which of their results is reported, and when a silent period counts as measured.

Changes in version 1.4.6

  • A per-recording analysis record, and a group-level reporting assessment built from it. Every first-level run now writes a record of what it measured and how, carrying everything derivable rather than only what a checklist asks for, together with the tool and detector versions that produced it. A group-level add-on reads those records and assesses the study against the TMS-RAT v1.0 reporting checklist, emitting the checklist in its own output format, the filled workbook, and a draft methods section. The assessment is done at study level because the checklist is: it rates one protocol within one study, and half its quantitative items are rated complete only when a central tendency and a dispersion are both reported, which no single recording can supply. Nothing is invented. An item the tool cannot know is reported as missing and names the fact that is absent, and the methods draft carries an explicit marker at every such point rather than reading smoothly around it.
  • The assessment refuses rather than averaging where averaging would mislead. Recordings analysed under different detector versions are not pooled at all: the same recording yields a different onset under a different detector, so a pooled mean would describe no analysis that was ever run. A value that differs across the study, such as two filter settings or three sampling rates, is reported as an analysis fault rather than as a missing field, because the majority value is not the answer and choosing it would hide both possibilities. An evoked response is reported per condition and never pooled across them, an M-wave averaged with a motor evoked potential being an amplitude nothing produced. An inter-trial interval whose standard deviation exceeds its mean is reported as not summarised by a mean, which is what a blocked design looks like when the gap between blocks is counted as an interval.
  • A recording's stimulus codes are now read from the file itself, whatever the format. Scanning was available for Spike2 native files alone, so every other format fell back to the shared stimulus marker label and offered a single code for a recording that might hold six, with nothing indicating that the list was a fallback rather than the file's contents. A LabChart MATLAB export holding two named triggers showed one; a Signal export holding six states showed one. Codes are now enumerated for every format, through the same call the analysis itself makes, so the table cannot offer a code the analysis would not find nor hide one it would. Where a format keeps its events in one place there is no channel to choose and none is offered.
  • A single recording may record a deviation from a stimulation parameter set. A session collected at a different intensity from the protocol could previously be described only by creating a second set, which reads as two protocols deliberately run rather than one protocol and one drift, and which of those is true is precisely what a reporting checklist exists to establish. A deviation is now recorded against the recording, applied to the sidecar it publishes and to the analysis record alike, listed before conversion and marked in the worklist. The set itself is unchanged and every other recording keeps the protocol value.
  • Native originals may be moved into sourcedata rather than copied. Off by default and confirmed when enabled. A file is removed only after its copy is in place, verified by size, and the converted file has been read back and matched; one that fails to verify keeps its original, which is exactly when the native file is still needed. Multi-file formats have their companions removed only where each has been copied. The file queue and the conversion worklist are re-pointed to the new location, an entry left naming a deleted path being indistinguishable from the tool having lost the recording.
  • participants.tsv is written with the columns BIDS defines. A file carrying only participant identifiers is valid and useless: nothing downstream can distinguish a study that did not record age from one where nobody added the column. Age, sex and handedness are now always present, as n/a where unknown, with a participants.json describing them and their permitted values.
  • sourcedata is placed beside rawdata rather than inside it. Both arrangements are valid BIDS; mixing them is not, and native files inside the raw dataset sit within every recursive search of it. An existing sourcedata folder is left where it is, a study half-converted under each rule being worse than one consistently under the old.
  • Smaller changes. The file queue gains status, format and free-text filters, with the count of what is shown stated at all times. Files that cannot be read are named with the reason rather than dropped from a folder scan in silence. A comma-separated table of numbers is no longer identified as a Spike2 text export. The list of formats the tool can open is derived in one place rather than restated at each dialogue, three copies of it having previously had to be edited together.
  • The data range for analysis is chosen per channel. It was one selection for the recording, applied to every channel analysed from it, which cannot express what a multi-channel recording usually needs: a block that is clean on the contralateral electrode is often unusable on the ipsilateral one, and the two are the same protocol recorded twice. Ranges are now held per channel and the picker shows each channel's own trace, its own events and its own selection, with an option to apply one selection to every channel for the common case where the usable block is the same because it is the same block. The window states where every channel stands at all times, a channel never opened there being analysed whole, which is a legitimate choice and an easy accident that were previously indistinguishable. The range in force reaches the analysis, the Conditions tab and the preview through one resolver, four independent readings of it being how a table came to number its trials from one channel's selection while the analysis numbered them from another's.
  • A range selects TRIALS rather than truncating the recording. An epoch needs signal before the stimulus and after it, so a range dragged to end just after the last pulse -- the natural way to draw one -- left that pulse without enough data and the trial was dropped. Every channel lost its last trial, and its first as well where the range began at a stimulus, with nothing said: the picker counted twenty events and the run measured nineteen. The signal kept is now padded by the epoch requirement while the stimuli are chosen from the range exactly as drawn, the padding never being analysed as a trial.
  • Conditions are recorded against the stimulus time, for every event in the recording. The events file was written from the trials of whichever channel the Conditions tab was displaying, and the analysis reads that file exclusively where it exists -- so an event with no row in it was not an unconditioned trial but no trial at all. With per-channel ranges this emptied every channel whose range differed from the one last displayed. Each event now carries a row, conditions assigned on any channel are kept for the trial rather than for the channel that happened to be on screen, and a condition assigned while viewing one channel is found by every other channel whose range contains that stimulus. The Conditions table still shows only the selected data.
  • The preview asks which channel to show. It followed the channel dropdown in the header, which chooses the channel being configured; on a study analysing four channels of thirteen that is a different question, and previewing a second channel meant leaving the preview, changing a control that also re-points the setup table, and coming back. It also reports how many events fell inside the selected range and how many of those lie within the loaded signal, so that a preview finding nothing says which of the two is zero.

Note on data ranges: any analysis that used a selected data range should be re-run. The trial at each edge of a range was silently excluded from the results, and on a multi-channel recording every channel was cut to the range chosen for whichever channel was on screen when the selection was made. A recording analysed with no range selected is unaffected.

Changes in version 1.4.5

  • Silent period values from version 1.4.4 and earlier were wrong, in the short direction, and analyses reporting them should be re-run. Three places measured the silent period and each built the detector's arguments itself. The Data Inspector capped the search end at the response plus the maximum-offset setting, which bounds where the silent period may start rather than where it may end, so at that setting's default no silent period longer than about a hundred milliseconds could be found during review while the analysis reported the true duration for the same trial. The preview built its configuration without a single numeric silent-period setting, so all of them fell back to defaults and the interface had no effect on it at all: changing the minimum EMG-return duration from forty milliseconds to two produced a byte-identical preview. All three now call one function with one settings object, and the search begins at each trial's own second peak-to-peak landmark everywhere. The fixed search-start setting has been removed, nothing having read it but the preview, and it is not retained as a floor because short-latency stimulus types reach their second peak well before its former default and a floor would begin the search after a genuine early silent period had already started.
  • The minimum EMG-return duration is now applied. It was carried through the interface, the configuration and every call, and never read, so breakthrough EMG partway through an otherwise complete silent period ended the measurement at the first burst. A value shorter than the smoothing window cannot be enforced, a moving root-mean-square envelope being unable to rise and fall faster than its own window; such a value is raised to the window and the trial says so rather than appearing to work. This is easily reached at high sampling rates, where the two quantities are set in milliseconds and compared in samples.
  • The silent period is measured on every trial of an enabled stimulus type. Its columns were populated only from stored review metadata, so a trial nobody had opened carried no silent period and the column described review history rather than the condition; on one twenty-trial condition this appeared as nine, seventeen or twenty trials depending on how much of it had been clicked through. The analysis now detects it directly, through the same entry point the review window uses. Stored markers still take precedence, a landmark placed or checked by hand being a decision that detection must not overrule.
  • Landmarks record whether they were detected or placed by hand, and each segment records which detector version produced its automatic markers. The two were previously indistinguishable, which mattered as soon as the detector changed: markers written by the previous version sat in the session and were reused verbatim, and discarding them wholesale would have destroyed genuine manual edits alongside them. Automatic markers from a superseded detector are now re-detected and manual edits kept. Sessions written before this release carry no provenance and cannot be attributed, so their markers are all re-detected; a manual edit made before this release will need placing again, which is the cost of not silently reporting a stale measurement.
  • Rectified and root-mean-square envelope overlays in the Data Inspector. The envelope drawn is the one the detector thresholded, built with the same function and the same window, and is shown with its suppression threshold, the baseline that threshold was derived from and the percentage between them, so that a marker can be judged against what produced it rather than against the raw trace the detector never examines. It is drawn mirrored about zero, a one-sided envelope colliding with the response's positive peak where the peak-to-peak markers must stay legible. Both are display only: which trace a marker is measured on is a property of the marker rather than of what happens to be visible.
  • Smaller corrections. The silent-period duration column was written as the text Not Marked where a trial had none, which made the whole column textual while the three columns beside it stayed numeric, so that one of the four was typed differently on reading and a mean over it returned a missing value without complaint; it is left empty now. Area under the curve is computed whenever the response has a detected end, whether that end came from a return to baseline or from the start of a silent period, the window having previously been closable only by the former so that trials whose silent period was detected rather than stored lost the measure silently. A silent period whose end was not observed before the search window closed is reported as a lower bound rather than as a measurement equal to the window width. A filter helper whose name described a return type it never had is renamed, the former name still resolving. An unreachable duplicate of the detection module has been removed.

Changes in version 1.4.4

  • Every chosen trial of a condition can be seen on one plot. The preview showed one trial at a time, which answers whether the markers landed sensibly on that trial and cannot answer whether a setting suits the condition. The second question is about a distribution -- whether onsets cluster or scatter, whether the amplitude window contains the response on most trials or only the large ones, whether one trial is unlike the rest -- and no single trial shows any of it, while stepping through eighty turns a distribution into a memory test. The preview now draws the chosen trials together, with the amplitude window the analysis resolved, the pre-stimulus window the baseline measures are computed over, and a strip beneath carrying one tick per onset, offset and silent-period end. Trials are chosen from a list beside the plot, and the traces may be rectified for display. Above sixty traces the drawing becomes a band of the per-sample minimum and maximum with the median over it, because a subsample of trials hides the outlier and the outlier is what an overlay is read for. Rectification is applied before the median, a rectified average being the average of the rectified trials rather than the rectified average of the raw ones; the two differ wherever trials disagree in sign, which on a biphasic response is most of the epoch. Conditions cut to different epochs are refused rather than drawn together, since one time axis cannot describe two, and the differing epochs are named rather than the option quietly missing. The overlay and the trial-by-trial view share one window and one event-type control: as two windows with two dropdowns they could disagree, and one showing a different stimulus type from the other reads as the two contradicting each other. Approach adopted from the TMS Analysis ToolBox (Cunningham et al.), which overlays a condition’s trials for the same purpose; written independently.
  • Four settings the preview was not reading. Each was silent: the preview reported a number, the number looked plausible, and it had been derived without a setting the analyst had changed. The blanking gap and the silent-period assignment never reached it, so a gap set to 50 ms had no visible effect anywhere and the end of a response was found by return-to-baseline on stimulus types where a silent period defines it. The window drawn as the pre-stimulus baseline was the wrong one of the two the analysis cuts: the epoch’s own lead-in, which the onset detectors threshold against, rather than the separate segment ending a gap before the stimulus that PreStimRMS, PreStimPTP, the outlier screen and the excitability compensation are computed from. It was also resolved once across every stimulus type in the file, taking the largest gap, so one type’s 20 ms gap displaced the shaded window on every other type in the recording. And silent-period detection could not run at all, two faults in one call leaving it to report that none was found whatever had been configured. The detector’s own account of why it found nothing is now reported, along with the window it searched, and a type with no silent period assigned is distinguished from one assigned and not found.
  • Offsets and silent periods are now found with the analysis’s own detectors before the preview opens, as onsets already were, so the trial-by-trial view shows the landmarks the run will produce rather than re-deriving them one trial at a time. The silent period is found first, because the offset rule takes a detected silent-period start as the end of the response: the two are one physical event, and the other order reports a return to baseline on exactly the trials where a silent period exists.
  • A fault in that stage no longer discards the onsets. It shared the onset stage’s error handler, which empties the seed, so a silent-period problem cost the onsets that had already been found -- and the symptom was an empty onset strip beside a trial view showing a perfectly good latency, which points at the wrong stage entirely.
  • The count of pre-detected onsets counted the wrong thing. The seed now also holds offsets and silent periods, which exist for trials whose onset detection found nothing, so a type with six onsets and twenty silent periods was reported as twenty of twenty. That line is read to judge whether a detection setting is working, and an inflated one is worse than none: the figure moved between two runs whose detection had not changed at all.
  • Results are now grouped by output family. One recording writes nine files per channel, so a two-channel study left eighteen loose files in one folder and a five-channel study forty-five, before any add-on. The folder stopped being readable long before the study stopped being ordinary. Results are now filed under trial-level, summary, onset-methods, segments, add-ons and report, grouped by what a file IS rather than by which channel produced it, so that an analyst comparing a measurement across channels has them side by side and the number of folders is fixed by what the tool writes rather than growing with the recording. Filenames do not change: a file has to be identifiable from its name wherever it ends up, so the full BIDS prefix is kept even though it is redundant inside a folder that already implies part of it. Nothing is moved. An existing study keeps the flat layout it was written with, both arrangements are read, and a folder half in each state loads completely.
  • An optional trimmed copy of the trial file. The trial-level table carries fifty-six columns. Every one is there because some study needed it, but a table nobody can read across on one screen is a table whose columns get selected in a spreadsheet by hand, which is where transcription errors come from. A run may now also write _trials_selected.csv beside the full file, holding a chosen subset: the same one row per trial, narrower. Columns are chosen by group rather than individually, because nobody keeps three of the four detrended columns, and a group whose members are uninterpretable without another pulls it in and says so in the log. _trials.csv is never affected and always carries every column; the narrowing happens on a copy at the moment of writing, and the positional row schema behind the analysis is neither read nor reordered by it. Nothing is lost by using the trimmed file: the columns that identify a trial are always kept, so it can be merged back against the full one whenever a dropped column is wanted. Off by default. The choice of columns is a preference applying to every recording, and a single recording may override it, with “leave it at the default” kept distinct from “off here” so that switching the preference on later cannot quietly switch a recording back on.
  • The group analysis states what its table contains. It may be built from either trial file. Where the trimmed file is asked for, sessions that lack one, or that did not select the same columns, are named and the build is refused rather than completed from whatever each session happens to have; a table whose columns depend on which participants were included is one where adding a participant silently changes the analysable variables, and the difference would arrive as blanks indistinguishable from a measurement that failed. Sessions are compared on the selection each recorded at analysis time rather than on their file headers, which cannot tell an analyst who chose to drop a measure from a recording that had none. Add-on outputs, which were joined unconditionally, may now be excluded or chosen individually; the choices offered are discovered from what is present beside the scanned sessions, so a third-party add-on appears without being known to the tool, and one present in only some sessions says so before it is chosen. The trial file source and the add-on choices are saved with the study design, a study rebuilt under different ones being a different table.
  • Add-on outputs are written to their own folder. They are the reason a results folder grows without bound and the files an analyst is least likely to be hunting for, so they are filed together rather than scattered among the core outputs. The results folder given to an add-on now means the results root and is read-only, which is what an add-on reading another's output already assumed it was.
  • 1.4.2 corrects the analysis window used by several measurements. Since per-stimulus-type epoch windows were introduced, five places in the analysis were given the file-wide window while working on a segment cut to a stimulus type's own window. Where a condition used a different epoch from the file-wide setting, this displaced the peak-to-peak markers, the MEP offset and duration, and the onset search. Latency was unaffected, which is what made it hard to see: a results file could carry correct latencies beside amplitudes measured over the wrong interval, including impossible negative values. Studies whose stimulus types all share one epoch window are NOT affected, because the two windows were the same number. Anyone who set a per-condition or per-type epoch should reprocess.
  • The Data Inspector no longer reuses landmarks the geometry has moved under. Peak, onset and offset markers are positions in a segment, and applying an event delay or changing an epoch moves the response while the stored positions stay put. Landmarks are now recorded with the geometry that placed them and re-detected when it changes.
  • Reporting says what it means. A non-detection caused by the minimum-amplitude gate names the gate and where to change it; the preview reports detected onsets as a fraction and counts hand-placed ones separately; an unanchored amplitude window says so; an impossible peak-to-peak is reported as a fault rather than printed; and a value outside a closed NIBS-BIDS vocabulary is named at conversion.
  • Smaller fixes: the TMSMultiLab mark appears in compiled builds again (the asset path was not resolved inside a frozen bundle) and is redrawn from a high-resolution original; a Spike2 channel unit the quantities library cannot parse, such as Nm, is preserved rather than recorded as dimensionless; and the stimulation description is written as *_nibs.tsv rather than a per-modality filename, which is what a BIDS validator looks for.
  • 1.4.1 is a maintenance follow-up to 1.4.0, released the same day. It changes nothing an analyst will see: the continuous integration suite installed a hand-written subset of the project's dependencies rather than the declared ones, so it reported failures on a release whose shipped code was correct. The path rules for locating a recording's derivatives also moved out of the application module, so that converting a file no longer requires importing the graphical interface. Everything below was introduced in 1.4.0.
  • The licence changes to the GNU General Public License version 3. Versions 1.3.3 and earlier were released under the MIT Licence and remain so; that grant cannot be withdrawn, and anyone who obtained those releases keeps the rights they were given. From this version the project is GPL-3, which was necessary in order to incorporate work derived from the TMS Analysis ToolBox (Cunningham, Zhang and Cahn, 2021), a GPL-3 project whose terms require derivative works to carry the same licence. The practical consequence is that software which incorporates this one must also be distributed under GPL-3; use of the application to analyse data, and publication of results obtained with it, are unaffected.
  • The epoch window is now set per stimulus type. The interval cut around each stimulus, and shown in the data inspector, is a property of the response rather than of the recording: a cortical silent period requires several hundred milliseconds after the pulse, an M-wave a few tens, and one shared window meant truncating the first or carrying an order of magnitude of unnecessary samples through every trial of the second. Pre- and post-stimulus extents appear as columns on the labels tab, seeded from a preference and following it while left unedited. The former file-wide fields have been removed from the feature detection tab, where neither was display-only despite being labelled so and one additionally set the inspector's zoom; what remains there is the baseline given to the detectors, which genuinely is one setting for the recording. A file whose stimulus types share a window behaves exactly as before. Windows are shortened to fit a pre-epoched recording, and the shortening is reported rather than applied silently, because a window reaching past the stored epoch draws its baseline from the previous trial's response.
  • Preview detection. Detection settings can be tried on chosen trials before committing to a run. The preview reads its settings from the same snapshot the analysis takes, cuts trials with the same epoching and event delay, and opens the ordinary data inspector read-only, so markers are drawn where the detector places them but cannot be dragged and nothing is written. Trials are chosen from a list defaulting to an even spread across the session rather than the first few, the opening trials being where a participant is freshest and least informative about whether a setting is right. Two things a preview cannot reproduce are stated rather than hidden: amplitude window anchoring is computed from a completed run, and outlier decisions do not exist yet.
  • Configured event sources now reach the analysis. Sources were previously read only to populate the labels tab, so a configured threshold changed what was displayed while the analysis went on reading the file's own markers by name. They are held per channel, since a trigger that is clean on one electrode can sit near the noise floor on another and a bilateral protocol has a separate stimulator per limb, and they are recorded in the derivative sidecar so a run states how its stimuli were identified. The dialogue that configures them now previews every kind of source, with a whole-recording view and a single-event view that can be stepped through or jumped to by number.
  • CED Signal MATLAB exports are read. Frames are treated as pre-epoched trials, with the frame state becoming the stimulus type and the stored epoch reported so analysis windows are clamped to it. These files are written in MATLAB version 7.3, which the older MATLAB readers cannot open, so h5py is now a dependency and is bundled into the pre-built binaries. The reader was written from the files themselves rather than from any other toolbox's source.
  • Every setting on the labels and feature detection tabs carries its own explanation, shown by hovering over the marker beside it or clicking to keep it open. The prose that previously stood above those tables described a handful of settings each while occupying the vertical space the tables needed, and sat far enough from the fields that reading it meant holding a column name in mind. Where a setting's meaning depends on the state of another, the explanation follows that state.
  • Several channels may now be analysed from one recording. The analysis runs once per selected channel, in sequence, and each pass uses that channel's own configuration: labels, blanking gaps, event delays, silent period assignment, normalisation references and latency profiles. An ipsilateral silent period recorded on one channel and a contralateral motor evoked potential on another are different muscles responding to the same marker, and they require different latency windows; a single shared table could not express that. Channels are chosen when a Spike2 recording is first opened, in a dialogue that now offers a tick list rather than a single choice, or afterwards from a control beside the channel selector. No channel is designated primary, since every selected channel is analysed identically and a primary would imply a hierarchy that does not exist; the first selected is simply where configuration begins. The confirmation button steps through the selected channels in turn and the analysis will not start while any remain unconfirmed, so a channel cannot be selected and then forgotten. A channel not yet configured begins from defaults rather than inheriting the previous channel's table, because inheriting one silently is a way to apply another muscle's latency window without noticing. Where more than one channel is analysed the output filenames carry a channel entity so that the passes do not overwrite one another, and a channel column is written to the trial and summary files in every case, so that a single-channel result can still join a multi-channel dataset. The analysis pipeline itself is unchanged: it receives one channel's settings per run and knows nothing of the others.
  • Where stimulus events come from is now stated explicitly. Every reader exposed the same function for retrieving stimulation times, and every reader meant something different by its one argument: the event channel to read, the label to attach to threshold detections, or nothing at all. The shared signature was a coincidence of naming rather than an interface, so asking a reader for something it did not already do was impossible, the one parameter that could have carried the request having already been given another meaning. LabChart MATLAB files consequently yielded their comment table and nothing else, which was not so much a missing feature as a missing question: the format carries comments, digital inputs and fixed-interval sampling, and only the first could be asked for. Events are now drawn from an explicit list of sources of three kinds: the events the file already carries, whether comments, markers, annotations or event channels; a crossing on any analogue channel, specified by level, edge and a refractory period so that a pulse which rings is counted once; and fixed timing, for recordings triggered by something the file does not record. Several may be combined, each contributing its own stimulus type. Threshold and interval detection depend on nothing but a waveform and a time base, both of which every reader already provides, so they are implemented once and available to all of them; a reader need only declare which of its channels are analogue. The previous function is unchanged and is what a source of the first kind calls, so a file configured as every file was configured before passes through no new code, a contract verified against real recordings in six formats and against files the tests construct themselves in three more.
  • Two sources producing the same stimulus type is reported as an error; two producing events at nearly the same instant are kept and reported. Combining the former would give a trial count matching neither source, and a disagreement of that kind is far more likely to be a misconfiguration than an intention. The latter cannot be resolved from the data at all: a comment written by software immediately after a trigger pulse is indistinguishable from two genuine stimuli a few milliseconds apart, and merging them would silently halve the trial count of a paired-pulse protocol. Both circumstances are described in the log rather than absorbed.
  • A preview for choosing a threshold level. A level cannot be verified by reading it: two volts is correct or incorrect depending on the trigger's amplitude, its baseline and whether the pulse rings, none of which is apparent from the field in which it was typed. The chosen channel is now drawn with the level across it, every detected crossing marked, and a count that changes as the level does. The trace is reduced for display by taking the minimum and maximum of each displayed column rather than by subsampling: a stimulus trigger is a single-sample transient, and on a two-thousand-second recording sampled at five kilohertz, subsampling produced a flat line while the detector found two hundred events. A preview which conceals the pulses is worse than none, the level then being set against a trace showing nothing of what the detector responds to.
  • Several channels may be selected when a file is opened, and the assignment is shown every time. The channel assignment dialogue offered a single channel and appeared only when no saved assignment existed, so after the first opening the channel and trigger choices became invisible and unalterable; the only recourse was deleting the derivatives folder and the companion files by hand. These two decisions determine what the entire analysis measures. The dialogue now offers a list of tick boxes, appears whenever a file is opened with the previous choices already selected, and can be reset explicitly from the File menu. No channel is designated primary, every selected channel being analysed identically; the first selected is simply where configuration begins. Both of the tool's channel dialogues were changed, since multi-channel analysis is not a property of one file format and leaving the second as a single choice would have made the capability reachable in one format of ten.
  • Files no reader can open are identified rather than misattributed. Format detection concluded by assuming that anything unrecognised was a Spike2 text export, so a word-processor document, a configuration file or an ADInstruments native recording each failed at some later point with a message naming the wrong format. A binary file matching no known signature is now reported as unreadable, and where the extension is recognised the message states what to do instead.
  • Marker edits no longer cross between channels. A marker position is an index into one channel's waveform and means nothing when applied to another. In an analysis of several channels the second inherited the first's, which produced negative peak-to-peak amplitudes wherever the stored maximum sample fell below the stored minimum, and reported every offset as manually placed when none had been. Edits are now held separately per channel through the analysis, the interactive inspector and the session file. A session written before this change carries a single unattributed set; it is used for review of one channel, where it unambiguously belongs to the channel displayed, and disregarded in an analysis of several rather than assigned by guesswork. A negative peak-to-peak amplitude can no longer be written in any case: it is a magnitude, and the value had been propagating into the normalisation and standard-score columns as though it were meaningful.
  • A session saved by hand is now as complete as one saved automatically. The two were assembled separately and had diverged: the manual path recorded thirteen fewer settings, among them the latency profiles, both muscle-group selections, the onset detection method and every one of its parameters. Reloading such a session restored the file and most of its settings while silently reverting those, so a subsequent analysis could proceed with a latency window and a detector the analyst had not chosen, and nothing indicated it. Both paths now build the same payload. Analyses whose sessions were saved through the File menu should be checked.
  • A correction for event markers that do not coincide with the stimulus. The marker recorded in a file is not always the instant the stimulus fired: a trigger written by software after the pulse, a delay setting on the stimulator, or a different signal path for one block will each shift it, usually by a fixed amount. The consequence is not a visibly wrong latency but an epoch whose zero is wrong, so that part of the response falls into the pre-stimulus window and every measure defined relative to the baseline then fails, each in a manner resembling a separate fault. On one recording whose markers for a single condition were two milliseconds late, the derivative-ratio detector returned no onsets at all from fifteen trials, peak-to-peak amplitude was read from a shoulder rather than the peak, and the offset was reported part-way down a deflection; these were investigated as three unrelated problems before the common cause was identified. A per-stimulus-type delay is now applied when epoching, so that everything measured from zero moves with it, including reported latencies. The delay may be measured automatically from the stimulus artefact. The artefact is located by peak slope rather than peak amplitude, since it is the steepest feature in the epoch but not always the largest and an amplitude search returns the response instead on a supramaximal compound muscle action potential. Two conditions govern whether a delay is proposed at all. The first is the spread across trials: a genuine fixed delay measures a fraction of a millisecond in standard deviation, whereas markers that truly jitter measured 3.9 milliseconds on a real recording, and above a threshold the scan reports the spread and proposes nothing, a single correction being wrong on every trial rather than right on average in that case. The second is the width of the transient: where there is no artefact, the steepest feature is the response's own rising edge, which is consistent enough across trials to pass the spread test and would therefore be proposed with confidence, so a width limit distinguishes them — across two recordings the artefact measured 0.4 to 0.6 milliseconds wide at half its maximum against 4.6 milliseconds for a response edge. Nothing is applied silently: proposed values populate the interface for review, the value and whether it was measured or entered by hand are written to the sidecar, and altering a delay marks affected files as requiring reprocessing.
  • Three faults corrected in offset detection. First, the refinement stage reported its own search boundary. It scanned a fixed neighbourhood for the first sustained quiet interval, and where the fine envelope was already quiet at the start of that neighbourhood, which is the ordinary case because a centred coarse window places the crossing late, it returned the neighbourhood's lower bound. The reported offset was therefore the coarse crossing minus the envelope window on every trial: a function of a smoothing setting rather than of the signal. The refinement now walks back to the last sample that remained elevated, which removes the dependence on the search radius entirely; across envelope windows of three, five and eight milliseconds the offset now varies by six tenths of a millisecond where previously it moved with the setting. Second, the envelope baseline is now estimated by the median and median absolute deviation rather than the mean and standard deviation. The envelope is computed with a centred window, so a stimulus artefact smears backwards by half of it; the guard applied by the caller covers an artefact at zero, but one landing even slightly earlier reaches past it and a handful of contaminated samples then dominate the estimate. On a real recording this raised the return threshold seventy-three-fold relative to a neighbouring condition, and the offset was reported while the response was still at a quarter of its peak amplitude. Third, the peak-fraction floor beneath the return threshold is now disabled by default. It had been introduced to address a case in which offset detection failed on eighty of eighty-one trials, but the cause there was a sixty-millisecond duration ceiling, and once that was raised the baseline threshold alone detected every trial. What the floor does is shorten the reported offset, in proportion to the size of the response, so that it truncates most severely on the largest and cleanest responses; measured against an independent settling criterion on a real recording it shortened the offset by between forty-five and ninety-seven milliseconds depending on its value, whereas at zero the same criterion gave errors of minus 5.9 and plus 2.3 milliseconds. On a resting recording, where responses are an order of magnitude smaller, the two settings are indistinguishable.
  • The return threshold now accounts for where the signal settles. It had been derived from the pre-stimulus baseline alone, which assumes the signal returns to where it began. Measured across every condition of one session, the envelope floor late in the epoch stood between 1.3 and 2.0 times the pre-stimulus floor, so that the pre-stimulus level was a target the signal never reached and the offset was reported wherever the envelope happened to dip. The threshold is now the larger of the two. Across eight conditions of two recordings the median offset moved earlier in every case; trial-to-trial scatter improved in five and worsened in two.
  • Amplitude window anchoring falls back to the stimulus type's own latency profile. Where a stimulus type has too few detected onsets to anchor its measurement window, the fallback had been the file-wide window, which is the very setting that anchoring exists to replace and is typically placed after the peak of a compound muscle action potential. The condition already in difficulty was therefore also the one whose amplitude was truncated, while its neighbours measured correctly. On a real recording the first phase of a 3.8 millivolt response fell outside the window entirely and peak-to-peak amplitude was read from a 2.1 millivolt shoulder.
  • Data Inspector. The offset and the response duration are reported alongside the existing measures and update as markers are moved. Where a cortical silent period is detected, its start marker is the offset marker, the two being one physical event; two draggable markers for a single event may be moved apart, and the file would then record two answers to the same question. The integration window for area under the curve is tied to the onset and the offset in both directions and is reconciled whenever a trial is displayed rather than only when a marker is moved; it had previously ended at a fixed fifty milliseconds after onset and could therefore disagree with the results file. A background silent-period search that set this window for every stimulus type, including resting recordings where the concept does not apply, no longer runs for types not assigned to silent period measurement. The amplitude measurement window is now taken from the analysis rather than re-derived from the file-wide setting, so that review and analysis measure the same interval when anchoring is enabled. A failed onset detection is reported as such: the marker had fallen back to the stimulus, which read as a latency of zero, and that index was returned on saving as a manual override, silently converting a blank latency into a measured one. An option displays the stimulus type's median waveform behind the trial, this being the same waveform the derivative-ratio detector compares each trial against.
  • Selecting a range of data now describes what the selection contains. The dialogue reported the selected intervals in seconds, which says nothing about the trials within them; a recruitment curve, a block at a fixed intensity and a silent period block may occupy one recording with no visible boundary between them. The selection is now described in trials: how many of each stimulus type, and their positions in the file's own numbering, which follows the same convention as the Data Inspector. A discontinuous selection is reported as the intervals it comprises rather than collapsed to its outer bounds, since collapsing would claim more trials than were chosen.
  • Smaller changes. The sampling rate and amplitude unit are reported when a file is opened; both were read automatically but neither was shown until the analysis ran, so that opening a file gave no confirmation of what had been detected. The filter preview accepts every format the readers handle, having carried its own list of extensions that was not updated when support for EDF, BrainVision, MATLAB, AcqKnowledge and delimited text was added; a MATLAB file consequently failed to load there and the preview requested a sampling rate the file had already declared. The guidance on the setup tab now states what the blanking gap does to the background window. Quitting no longer prints interface errors caused by callbacks left queued against an interpreter being torn down. A latency window that contradicts the muscle group selected alongside it is now reported, the previous symptom of the two disagreeing being onsets accumulating at the lower bound of a profile the interface was no longer displaying.
  • New onset detection method: derivative ratio, after Boyles et al. (2026). Working backwards from the first peak of the response, each candidate sample is scored by the ratio of the mean absolute derivative ahead of it to the mean absolute derivative behind it, and the onset is the earliest sample still reaching a set fraction of the largest such ratio. Three gates follow: a latency ceiling, a requirement that most of the first few forward derivatives exceed the baseline mean derivative, and a requirement that the mean derivative over a following window exceed the baseline mean by a multiple of its standard deviation. The method is independent of every other detector in the tool in what it measures, being neither a threshold crossing, nor a run length in the derivative, nor a cumulative change point, and that independence is its principal value as a member method. Ported from the MATLAB reference implementation in the TMSMultiLab library. Off by default and not among the default member methods.
  • Detectors may now be supplied with a condition average. The derivative-ratio method requires a grand-mean waveform in order to reject trials whose peak falls far from the expected latency. The analysis supplies the outlier-screened median waveform of each stimulus type, which is the same waveform onset anchoring already used and is now computed whether or not anchoring is enabled. No other detector consults it and none changes behaviour as a consequence. The Data Inspector supplies the same waveform, so that a trial is judged against the same landmark during review as during analysis.
  • Three details of the reference implementation are corrected, each reversible. The published MATLAB code contains three behaviours that its own comments contradict. Each is corrected by default and reproduced exactly by a single option, because a correction that cannot be disabled makes the published method impossible to reproduce, while one applied silently makes a result attributable to neither version. First, the slope comparison window is fixed in samples rather than in milliseconds. The paper states the width both as five samples and, in its figure legend, as two and a half milliseconds; the two agree only at the two kilohertz used in that study. The reference implementation indexes with the literal five, so the window is five samples however the data were sampled, giving two and a half milliseconds at two kilohertz, one millisecond at five kilohertz and half a millisecond at ten kilohertz. Measured on a real recording, detection under the sample-count behaviour fell from eighteen trials in twenty at one kilohertz to eleven in twenty at five kilohertz; at exactly two kilohertz the two versions return identical results. This tool uses the published duration. Second, the amplitude gate compares the response's peak-to-peak amplitude against the baseline maximum rather than the baseline peak-to-peak amplitude, and is therefore approximately half as strict as its name and comment imply. Third, the peak-jitter gate compares the trial's largest peak against the condition average's first peak; on a biphasic response whose second phase is the larger, those two quantities differ by the peak-to-trough interval on every trial, so the tolerance is expended on a definitional mismatch rather than on jitter. The paper does not state which landmark it intends, so this third item is a clarification rather than a correction.
  • A stated limitation of the new method. Every one of its gates is expressed in absolute derivatives, so what it requires is that the response be spectrally richer than the baseline, and not merely larger. Measured at the published window, detection of a smooth synthetic response fell from nineteen trials in twenty at a baseline noise of 0.012 millivolts to none at all at 0.020 millivolts, while the same response carrying harmonic content still gave sixteen in twenty; the root-mean-square envelope detector scored twenty in twenty throughout that range. Quiet resting recordings sit well inside the working range, a real recording with a pre-stimulus root-mean-square of 0.0034 millivolts yielding seventeen to eighteen trials in twenty per condition, but a noisy baseline or aggressive low-pass filtering will disable it, and it fails by returning nothing rather than a wrong latency.
  • Renamed: the “consensus” method is now “median across methods”. The former name implied that the agreed value was the correct one, which is precisely the inference the method's own outputs caution against: detectors sharing an assumption may be wrong together, and two of the members are not independent, one taking the other's answer as its starting point. The trial-level column Onset_Consensus(ms) becomes Onset_MethodsMedian(ms), with the corresponding renaming in the method comparison tables. Sessions and preference files written by the previous release continue to work: the former method key still resolves, and the renamed preference is carried across on first load.

Note on the epoch window: analyses whose stimulus types should not share one window will differ from earlier releases, and deliberately so. A recording left at its previous settings is unchanged, since an unset per-type window falls back to the file-wide pair. Where a type is given its own window, everything measured within it follows: peak-to-peak amplitude if the window previously truncated the response, offset and duration and area under the curve if they extended beyond it. On a pre-epoched recording a window longer than the stored epoch is now shortened to fit, where a previous release would have measured the mirror-padded guard band between stitched trials and reported it as recorded signal.

Note on reproducibility: recordings analysed with an earlier release should be reprocessed if offset, duration or area under the curve was used, and any analysis whose session was saved through the File menu should be checked against the settings it was intended to use. The three corrections to offset detection change the reported offset on most recordings, and duration and area under the curve follow from it. Peak-to-peak amplitude changes only for stimulus types whose amplitude window previously fell back to the file-wide setting because too few onsets were detected. Latency changes only for stimulus types given an event delay, which is not applied unless requested. Cortical silent period and normalisation measures are unaffected. The renaming described above changes column headings but no values; a script reading Onset_Consensus(ms) by name will require updating. Recordings analysed with version 1.3.2 or earlier should be reprocessed if onset latency or area under the curve was used, for the reasons given at version 1.3.3; those analysed with version 1.3.1 or earlier for the trial-level column alignment corrected in version 1.3.2; and those analysed with the excitability compensation in version 1.2.5 or earlier for the reason noted at version 1.2.8.
